title: How do you roll out a breaking database change with zero downtime?
description: Expand-contract migrations: additive phases, backfills, dual writes, and cutover — changing schemas under live traffic without a maintenance window.

data.text: **Question:** How do you roll out a breaking database change with zero downtime?

Never do the breaking change as one migration — decompose it into the **expand-contract (parallel change)** pattern: **expand** (add the new nullable column/table/index alongside the old — additive, safe), **migrate** (backfill old data into the new shape in batches, run both writes or sync until caught up), **switch** (release code that reads the new shape; verify), then **contract** (drop the old column/constraint in a later deploy once nothing references it). Each phase is independently deployable and reversible, so the app never has a moment where old code can't run against the schema. The hard parts are the **backfill under load** (batched, throttled, resumable) and the **dual-write window** (kept as short as possible, ideally avoided via CDC or read-new-after-backfill).

**Why one-shot migrations break:**
- Rolling deploys mean old and new app versions run simultaneously — any schema change incompatible with either version breaks one of them
- Locking DDL (older MySQL ALTER, index builds on hot tables) can block writes for minutes
- Rollback of a destructive migration is impossible without backups — that's not a rollback plan

**The phases, concretely (rename column users.name → users.display_name as the cliché):**
1. **Expand**: `ALTER TABLE users ADD display_name varchar(200) NULL` — old code unaffected; new index built online (ONLINE/INPLACE on InnoDB, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on Postgres)
2. **Backfill**: batched updates — `UPDATE ... WHERE id BETWEEN @lo AND @hi`, thousands per transaction, throttled, resumable, checkpointed; or one-shot `ADD GENERATED` for computed columns
3. **Dual-write/switch reads**: app writes both columns (or single source + CDC sync), reads from the old until backfill verified, then flips reads to new behind a flag
4. **Verify**: row counts, checksum sampling, shadow reads comparing old vs new outputs in logs
5. **Contract**: remove dual-write code first (deploy), then drop the old column (deploy) — never the reverse; contract migrations ship versions after expand

**Tooling:**
- Online-safe DDL: Postgres (most ALTERs, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY), MySQL 8 instant/inplace algorithms; check the exact operation's locking behavior before running it on a hot table
- Backfill framework: batch size tuned to replica lag; pause on lag threshold; observable progress
- CDC (Debezium/trigger-based) to sync old→new without app dual-writes where available

**Rules of thumb:**
- Compatibility window: code must tolerate both schemas for the whole expand→contract span (days/weeks, not minutes)
- Every step reversible at its phase boundary; the only irreversible step (DROP) happens last, when risk is near zero
- Large table? Add the column, backfill over a week, *then* make it NOT NULL — never in one release

data.title: Rename + type change done with zero downtime
data.code:
Goal: users.name (varchar(100)) -> users.display_name (varchar(200), NOT NULL)

Release 1 (expand):
  ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN display_name varchar(200) NULL;   -- instant/online
  CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ix_users_display_name ON users(display_name);
  App: writes both name and display_name; still reads name. Deploy. Safe.

Job (backfill, runs days):
  loop batches: UPDATE users SET display_name = name
                WHERE id BETWEEN @lo AND @hi AND display_name IS NULL;
  throttle on replica lag > 500ms; checkpoint the high-water mark; resumable.

Release 2 (switch reads, behind flag):
  App reads display_name when present, falls back to name otherwise.
  Shadow-verify: log mismatches between old and new values; expect ~0.
  Flip flag globally when clean.

Release 3 (finalize):
  App: single-write to display_name only (drop dual write). Deploy.
  Then, much later:
Release 4 (contract):
  ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN name;                       -- now zero references

❌ The one-shot: ALTER ... RENAME in one deploy -> during rolling update,
   old pods (expecting 'name') crash until the fleet completes. Outage.
❌ Backfilling 200M rows in a single UPDATE -> locks, WAL flood, replica death.

data.title: The contract phase is where patience pays
data.text: Teams drop the old column 'a few days later' — and miss a mobile client from last quarter, a forgotten cron, or an analytics job that still selects it. Let contract wait until monitoring shows zero references to the old shape for a full business cycle, and make DROP fail loudly rather than silently in the next deploy.

items: Assuming rolling deploys tolerate a rename — old and new code need a compatibility window
Single-transaction backfills on huge tables — locks and WAL spikes
Deploying contract in the same release as expand — no observation window
Dual writes without an end condition — they live forever and drift
Ignoring non-app consumers: jobs, BI pipelines, reports selecting the old column
No resumability in backfill jobs — a crash restarts a week of work

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Expand → migrate/backfill → switch reads → contract, each its own deploy
Every phase tolerates both old and new code; only DROP is irreversible, so it goes last
Backfills are batched, throttled, resumable, and observable
Verify with shadow reads/checksums before flipping; wait a full cycle before contract
data.takeaway: Zero-downtime schema change means no single moment where one code version can't run — decompose the breaking change into additive steps and let time do the locking for you.
